Finally, when the barbarous race of the Saracens occupied the Holy Land, they devastated most things, erased the traces of Christian life, and changed almost the very face of the Holy Land; there can be no doubt that they also brought violence against the cave of Christ's nativity and seized the gold and other most precious ornaments with their own rapacious hands, so that many things which are shown there today are, if not counterfeit, at least uncertain. These things would have to be explained at greater length if they did not seem to exceed our allotted space. We therefore leave this stony cave of Christ's nativity, and we take our newborn <term>JESULUM</term> <gloss>little Jesus</gloss> with us from it, and, bound in the swaddling clothes of pure faith, we place him in the humble cave of our heart—thoroughly renewed and carved from the rock by the firmness of good purpose—adorning it not with gold or marble, but seasoning it with the myrrh of serious repentance, which is mildly bitter and of most sweet odor before God.

At the beginning of chapter VIII of John, as said above, the story of the Adulterous Woman is omitted, nor, however, is there any doubt that it is a genuine and Canonical part of the New Testament Scripture, whatever Hugo Grotius and Theodore Beza might contradict. We congratulate ourselves, however, that the Clause of the Lord's Prayer (which the Latin Vulgate edition does not acknowledge, and Robert Bellarmine and Maldonatus contend was added and inserted into the Evangelical text by the Greeks) exists in this version at Matthew VI, verse 13. Likewise, that the word *Jeremiah* is read in it at Matthew chapter XXVII, verse 9, which D. Au fond de quelques ouadis, émergent des calcaires argileux blancs, en blocs hauts de un à deux mètres et longs de quatre à six mètres.
10h 10 soir, campé.

15 mai. — 4h 40 matin, en route. Traversé plusieurs cuvettes restreintes, à des altitudes variables, donnant l'impression d'un steppe ondulé.
6h matin, passé à Bou Foumin sans s'arrêter. Le puits ayant été restauré quelques jours avant, les guides peuvent se procurer un peu d'eau. Profondeur du puits, 8 brasses (13 mètres environ). Bou Foumin est l'appellation arabe; les Tédas disent Kollori (Killori de Nachtigal). Après Bou Foumin, on entre dans le Manga.
7h 35 matin, halte dans un bon pâturage d'askanit. Les chameaux, qui n'ont pas rencontré cette plante depuis l'Azbin, s'en régalent.
2h 50 soir, en route. Trois kilomètres après la halte, les ouadis cessent; on fait route sur un plateau sans relief sensible, à l'altitude du sommet des dunes précédentes. La végétation herbacée diminue progressivement. A 20 kilomètres environ vers l'Ouest, aperçu une ligne de hautes dunes s'éloignant vers le Nord-Ouest.
Rencontré deux troupeaux d'antilopes mohor (*euryx leucoryx*).
10h 24 soir, campé. Rares touffes d'herbe.

16 mai. — 4h 04 matin, en route. La végétation herbacée diminue de plus en plus et bientôt on ne trouve que quelques rares pieds de bou rekkeba (mrokba) et de shep (?)<note>(1)</note>.
Très espacés : des talhas, des sarahs (serrahs), du r'tem, souvent sec.
Le sol est de sable à petits grains de gravier.
Très faibles ondulations du terrain, normales à la direction générale de la route. 6h 26 matin, les guides signalent qu'on arrive à la limite de la végétation arbustive. Comme on n'aperçoit d'herbe nulle part, halte pour faire manger les chameaux. Tout le long de l'étape précédente, petites rides de sable normales à la direction générale des vents (E. N. E. et E. q. N. E.).
Nombreuses traces d'antilopes; très peu de gibier en vue.
2h 49 soir, en route. Les arbres se font plus rares : quelques toumdoubs (*capparis sodada*), des sarahs, peu de talhas; herbes par touffes.
Terrain légèrement ondulé normalement à la direction générale de la route. 3h 53, apparition du hâd.
A partir de 5h environ, le sol est couvert de petits monticules de sable élevés par le vent à l'abri de chaque arbuste ou de chaque touffe d'herbe.
9h 27, campé en un point à peu près entièrement privé de végétation.

<note>(1) Cette plante n'a pu être identifiée.</note>

## ABSOLUTION

<margin>11.</margin>It is asked: Which of the words of absolution: *I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit*, belong to the essence of the form, and are necessary for the validity of the sacrament?

Answer: Although the learned doctors <note>theologians</note> disagree among themselves, and others have written that these words, *from your sins*, are only of the necessity of a precept and do not pertain to the essence of the form, and teach that these words are sufficient: *I absolve you*; nevertheless, it cannot be denied that there is greater probability in the opinion stating that those words, *from your sins*, also pertain to the essence of the form. For that is the opinion of the majority, and it seems to be gathered from the Council of Trent, session 14, chapter 3. Especially because those words, *I absolve you*, are indifferent to absolution from *sins and censures*. Therefore, so that they may signify specifically absolution from *sins*, they must be determined by these: *from your sins*. Since, therefore, that opinion is safer, undoubtedly he who omits them exposes the Sacrament to the danger of nullity, because when dealing with the validity of the sacraments, the safer path must always be followed according to the decree of Innocent XII condemning proposition 1.

It is written, "For those who know Your name will trust in You." And it is written, "As for me, may my prayer be to You, O Lord, at a favorable time." Now, a "favorable time" is the revelation of the Supreme Will. The revelation of this Will is the aspect of the expansion of light. The expansion of light is the revelation of Divinity. The revelation of Divinity is the expansion of Wisdom. The expansion of Wisdom is the revelation of Understanding. The revelation of Understanding is the expansion of Loving-kindness. The expansion of Loving-kindness is the revelation of Might. The revelation of Might is the expansion of Splendor. The expansion of Splendor is the revelation of Victory. The revelation of Victory is the expansion of Glory. The expansion of Glory is the revelation of Foundation. The revelation of Foundation is the expansion of Kingdom. The expansion of Kingdom is the revelation of the Divine Presence. The revelation of the Divine Presence is the aspect of the expansion of light. The expansion of light is the revelation of Divinity. The revelation of Divinity is the expansion of Wisdom. The expansion of Wisdom is the revelation of Understanding. The revelation of Understanding is the expansion of Loving-kindness. The expansion of Loving-kindness is the revelation of Might. The revelation of Might is the expansion of Splendor. The expansion of Splendor is the revelation of Victory. The revelation of Victory is the expansion of Glory. The expansion of Glory is the revelation of Foundation. The revelation of Foundation is the expansion of Kingdom. The expansion of Kingdom is the revelation of the Divine Presence.

<summary>This page describes a cascading sequence of divine emanations, beginning with the Supreme Will and extending through the Sefirot to the Divine Presence.</summary>

it can be much less of a wonder if the same should happen to the <term>unicornu</term>, which has indeed lacked a more accurate censure until now, besides that which was applied by the common people in their time, which, through longer progression, induces obscurity even in the most clear matters due to negligence. This eventually became all the greater because it is found very rarely and only in the treasuries of great princes. All of which could certainly have given the curious an opportunity to mix the true with the false, so that they might—if not substitute—at least admit into the place of the true <term>unicornu</term>, which they felt was held in delight by the magnates, fragments of perhaps burned horn, ivory, or other bones, or some kind of stones. In order for us to avoid such fraud, certain of the following signs seem entirely worthy of observation. But here, prudence and counsel are needed again, lest we seize upon and swear by false or superstitious things that are circulated as true and indubitable. Just as it is believed by the common people that the <term>unicornu</term> sweats in the presence of poison. Now, indeed, if it is asked whether and in what way it can happen that it emits a true sweat, the matter is quite stuck. To sweat is certainly an intrinsic effect excited by the benefit of the soul, and the <term>unicornu</term>, insofar as it is torn from the body and applied to medicine, lacks that soul; whence, therefore, the effect? Must one have recourse to occult qualities? But truly, neither do these act above their powers. Andreas Baccius, in the cited place, indeed reports that the horns of the <term>cerastes</term> <gloss>a species of snake</gloss> (a certain kind of snake, of which Albertus Magnus, Ulysses Aldrovandus, Lord Johannes Veslingius in Bartholinus, page 6, Jonston, and others make mention) as well as a certain kind of stone, of a glaucous, dark color, which they call "serpentine tongue," sweat in the presence of poison, but analogically or improperly; just as we see all polished and bright objects, surrounded by the humidity of the air, when heat approaches, altered in a certain way and as if emitting a sweat. But since that effect, or dimming, happens from elsewhere, even in the absence of poison, we are not to take it as some indubitable sign.

17. The same will hold if those who grant a delay are fewer in number but stronger in the quantity of debt, so that although only one of the creditors, to whom a sum larger than the rest is owed, has granted the <term>Inducias</term> <gloss>a stay of execution/moratorium</gloss>, he alone is to be heard according to the cited law: last, Code, *Who may surrender their goods*; see the reason in law 8, *On Pacts*, where Gothofredus <note>Jacques Godefroy, a 17th-century jurist</note> [writes]; Brunemann, in the same place; see the cited law in Mevius, chapter of the treatise, chapter 3, number 98. §. 6. 7. In all the aforementioned cases, however, when the question concerns the number of creditors, one should not look so much to their persons as to the sum of the debt itself. Therefore, if there are several debtors to whom one and the same sum is owed, and they are <term>correi</term> <gloss>joint debtors</gloss> with respect to that one debt, they are considered as one debtor only: law 10, *On Pacts*. Thus also, if several guardians of a ward have demanded a debt, they sustain the role of only one person, according to the cited law: Straccha, chapter of the treatise, page 6, number 10; Vander, chapter of the treatise, chapter 6, number 12; Mevius, in the cited place, number 105. <summary>This page details the legal procedures for weighing creditor votes in a moratorium (Inducias), establishing a hierarchy of decision-making based on debt sum, headcount, and judicial authority when disputes occur.</summary>

### DE IACA.

<margin>Iacę natales.</margin> Nascitur arbor in nonnullis India insulis secundum aquas, quæ licet nullum medicum usum præbeat, propter amplitudinem tamen, & fructus elegantiam, minimè prætermittenda est.

<margin>Eius nomenclatura.</margin> Eam Malabarenses Iaca, Guzaratenses Panax, Canarini Panasu, Arabes Panax & Iaca nuncupant: Persæ mutato p. in f. Fanax.

<margin>Eius descriptio.</margin> Vasta est arbor, foliis palmaris amplitudinis prædita, dilutè virentibus, neruo crasso & duro per longitudinem excurrente: malum fert non è germinibus aut foliorum sede, quemadmodum aliæ arbores, sed ex ipso trunco maioribusque ramis nascens, longum, crassum, obscuriùs virens, crasso duroque cortice tectum, vndique veluti adamantum cuspidibus septo, quæ in spinam breuem, viridem, nigroque aculeo præditam desinunt, admodum similem Durionis spinæ, sed minimè acutam aut pungentem, tametsi minitari videatur.

27. The end of Adamic Theology is various: (1) One with respect to God, namely the general glory of God, since all things tend to the glory of God (Psalm 115:1). The special [end is] the Glory of the Paternal mercy, to which the grateful Adam assigns this life, and in it all theology: the Glory of the Messiah, through whom he procures and applies to himself mystical life, and theology itself, by true faith: the Glory of the divine Spirit, from whose illumination, motion, direction, and inspiration of things and words, he professes this theology: the Glory of divine Wisdom, of which not only the Protoevangelium is the offspring, but also the theology of Adam: the Glory of divine revelation, to which Adam owes all his theology, and this Compendium also: the Glory of the didactic, or divine information, which was of such efficacy that Adam was both the Auditor of theology and became its Doctor, and this redounds to the Glory of such a great Doctor, etc.

28. (2) Another with respect to Adam: both the fulfillment of the doctoral specimen, and the imitation of the principal Doctor, and the expedition of the works of his calling, and the administration of the office undertaken, and the information of Eve or even his posterity, and the preaching or propagation of theological or evangelical doctrine, and the excitation of Eve or even his posterity to imitation, etc.

29. Lest, however, we seem to have brought these prerequisites of Adamic Theology from a foreign wit, or to have bestowed or foisted them upon Adam beyond the mind and words of the text, or to have brought them into [the text] rather than drawing them from the sense of the words, we shall therefore, through a brief analysis, as of the <term>chesin</term> <gloss>position/arrangement</gloss> and <term>chresin</term> <gloss>use</gloss> of the words, appropriately apply all the praised chapters of the prerequisites to the words themselves. AND, it is said in the text (namely (a) from the occasion, revelation, precept, or obligation, as also from the information or illumination of Jehovah Elohim, as the Primary Cause; (b) according to the norm of the Protoevangelium, the divine mirror of spiritual life, or the first Compendium of Theology, as the mediate cause, Adam (as the Ministerial and Economic Cause) Called (pronounced and preached, by oral profession, as an external form, the Word of spiritual life in Eve, not only to analogy, but also harmony, and <term>idiopoian</term> <gloss>personal appropriation</gloss>, or the very applied Essence of the Protoevangelium, since no other life is proposed here than that which had been proposed in the Protoevangelium, as an internal form).

For the whole epistle must be read today before the writer's name occurs. Furthermore, God calls first by creating when He produces from not being to being. There are three things he treats in the whole epistle. In the beginning, he corrects in the <term>Corinthians</term> those vices which seemed light to them and not at all worthy of notice: therefore, they had not sought the Apostle's judgment on these. Because these were the gravest, he proposes them in the first place, such as were the dissensions and sects on account of teachers; the vain persuasion by which they sought eloquence in the ministers of the Lord; fornication; incest; and the habit of litigating before infidel judges. They cared little for these and similar things. These are treated up to the seventh chapter. In the second part, he responds to the questions of the <term>Corinthians</term>, which in good part were born from the contention of the teachers and had rendered the listeners ambiguous. Such are the questions moved concerning marriage in chapter 7; concerning the choice of foods, namely concerning things sacrificed to idols; concerning idols; and in chapter 11, concerning ecclesiastical assemblies and the avoiding of women. Also, lest they teach publicly, or rather, lest they have any right of questioning; concerning the <term>Supper of the Lord</term>; concerning the use of spiritual gifts; concerning the excellence of the prophetic office; concerning the <term>resurrection of the dead</term>, and the like up to chapter 16. In the third place, he attaches an appendix concerning private matters in the last chapter: concerning the collection, concerning his own arrival, concerning <term>Timothy</term>, and similar things which are private and did not greatly pertain to the matter of the writing.
